paper.title: Network Connections and Board Seats: Are Female Networks Less Valuable?
paper.code_data_availability: Verbatim (p. 324, n.): "Information concerning access to the data used in this paper is available as supplemental material online." The analysis uses administrative register data from Statistics Denmark and board data from the Danish …

registers.name_in_paper: Administrative register data from Statistics Denmark (employer-employee data on work histories)
registers.years: 1995-2011 (workplace information from 1992 onward, needed to build the 3-year network windows)
registers.role: sample frame; treatment (network construction); controls; outcomes for the qualification regressions
variables_mentioned: education level and education type (seven categories; STEM+ constructed)
share of women employed in the firm

registers.role: treatment and outcome: who sits on a board with whom in a given period, for individuals born in Denmark

linkages: Directors in the Danish Business Authority data are matched to their primary workplace in the Statistics Denmark data using an anonymous ID for each director
Individual workers are matched to the firms where they have their primary occupation

Coworkers are identified as individuals sharing a primary workplace; the four network measures are built from individual work histories (available since 1992) and from the board/executive status of those coworkers over the following 3 years
Board networks link a director to the other directors of every board on which the individual sits in a given year

sample.universe: All employed individuals aged 16-65 in the Danish labor market 1995-2011 whose main occupation is a management position (individuals who manage other people at their primary workplace); board data cover individuals born in Denmark
sample.unit_of_observation: individual-year (manager-year); for table 14, the first-time director in the year of appointment; for table 1 and figures, firms and director-years
selection_rules: Start from the administrative register work histories of all employed individuals aged 16-65, 1995-2011
Keep all individuals in the Danish labor market with any management position as their main occupation (new managers enter; managers who grow older than 65 stay in the sample)
Restrict the recruiting boards to firms with at least 50 employees, to avoid boards of firms without regular business activity (holding companies, small firms with informal board governance)
Exclude appointments to boards of public sector firms (managers in public sector firms are kept in the employer-employee data set)
Exclude the appointments of employee-elected board members
First-time-appointment sample: in each year keep the managers who have not yet served on a board; drop the individual after the first appointment; individuals appointed before 1995 are dropped
Any-appointment sample: keep the full set of managers, including those already appointed to one or more boards
Table 14 sample: the pooled set of first-time directors only
sample.n_observations: 4,230,150 individual-year observations in the full sample of managers (table 1); 4,003,953 in the first-time-appointment regressions; 4,230,150 in the any-appointment regressions; 20,144 first-time directors in table 14; 129,822 individual director observations; 56,161 firm observations with a board of directors
sample.n_individuals: Not reported as a count of persons; table 1 reports 185,976 individuals in 1995 and 305,309 in 2011, and 6,676 (1995) and 7,625 (2011) individual directors

construction_notes: Coworker board network at t: coworkers of the individual from his or her primary job at t-3 who, from t-3 and over the following 3 years, are already board members or get appointed to a board; the 3-year window captures the average tenure of a board position

Executive network at t: cumulative count of all connections to other top executives in past and present primary jobs until t; a positive value requires having held an executive position at least once from 1995 until t
Coworker executive network at t: coworkers from the primary job at t-3 who, from t-3 and over the following 3 years, are appointed to a top executive position in any firm

Board network at t: number of unique relations to the other board members of all boards where the individual is a director; positive only for individuals holding at least one board position; omitted from the first-time-appointment regressions
All network variables enter the regressions divided by 100 and lagged one year (measured at t-1)
Network variables are interacted with a dummy for being a woman; men are the reference group
Three management categories from Disco codes: CEO, other top executive (OTE), pool of potential (POP, management below the executive suite)
STEM+ = a STEM degree (science, technology, engineering, medicine) or a degree in economics, business or law
Family-run firm = two or more family members on the board of directors or in the executive suite; parents, children, married couples, siblings and cousins count as family
Large firm = more than 250 employees; medium-sized firm = 50-250 employees; only 3% of the firms in the sample are listed; 42% are family-run

Five industry categories (primary; manufacturing; trade and transport; finance and private services; other) and six occupational job categories (human resources; finance; sales; information technology and R&D; production; other) enter as fixed effects
Standard errors are clustered on the individual in tables 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14
Experience as an other top executive is excluded from the main regressions because it is highly correlated with the executive network variable
Appointment rates in table 2 and table 6 are scaled by 100 (reported in percent)

key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the authors instead compare pooled OLS with individual and firm fixed effects to show what different sources of variation imply, and restrict the sample to managers.

threats_discussed: Endogeneity of network formation (Manski 1993): no credible identification strategy, so the authors call the analysis descriptive and exploratory
Unobserved heterogeneity: individuals with a high ability to be recruited may also be better at forming valuable networks, e.g. through the choice of workplace
Time-variant omitted variables remain after individual or firm fixed effects
Selection of managers into the public sector, into family-run firms and into firms above or below median size differs by gender
Multicollinearity between the executive network variable and years of experience as a top executive
A linear probability model for a very rare binary outcome
Individuals who change their network connections may have qualities making them more appointable, so the within-individual estimates are driven by a selected group

Within, between and overall variation of the network variables reported (table A5)
Including experience as an OTE as a control leaves the results the same (results available on request, n. 10)
Expanding the table 14 sample to all appointments, not only the first (table A12)

definition.value: Interaction term: the dummy for being a woman multiplied by Coworker board network/100 (CBN/100). definition.value: Interaction term: the dummy for being a woman multiplied by Coworker board network/100 (CBN/100). Its coefficient is the gender difference in the association, i.e. the extra association for women relative to men (men are the reference group). Base variable: Number of coworkers of individual i from his or her primary job at time t-3 who, from t-3 and over the following 3 years, are already members of a board of directors or get appointed to one; entered in the regression divided by 100. key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the authors instead compare pooled OLS with individual and firm fixed effects to show what different sources of variation imply, and restrict the sample to managers.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 4 compares the sample of managers with the full Danish labor market; the authors assume the sample is year-by-year representative of the individual managers who have a chance of being appointed for the first time.
